USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current tariff posture and continue negotiations without further escalation or concession. The US has already imposed tariffs on $250B of Chinese goods and raised rates on $200B from 10% to 25%; additional escalation risks further harm to US consumers and supply chains, while conceding now would squander leverage. Hold firm and let Phase 1 talks proceed.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate but real. The UNCTAD study shows US tariffs have caused a $35B blow to Chinese exports but consumers in the US are bearing the heaviest brunt of higher prices (UNCTAD, 2019). White House adviser Larry Kudlow acknowledged 'both sides will suffer' (Fox Business, May 2019). The USC analysis warns that tariffs will raise costs for American consumers on everything from fish to furniture, and new cars could cost $1,000-$3,000 more (Annenberg/USC). The IMF has cut global growth forecasts partly due to trade tensions (BBC). However, the US also has leverage: China absorbed only 75% of its prior exports to the US despite substantial tariffs, showing vulnerability (UNCTAD). Senator Graham argues this is the best chance to change China's 'cheating ways' on IP theft and market access (Fox Business). The US trade deficit with China stands at $419B (BBC), and the core issues—IP theft, forced technology transfer, market access—remain unresolved. With Phase 1 talks ongoing and the tariff hike to 25% already in effect, the US should hold its current position rather than escalate further (which risks recession and ally defection to third-country suppliers) or concede (which would waste the leverage already built). The trade diversion effect—$21B flowing to Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, and the EU—partially offsets Chinese losses but also means US supply chains are already reconfiguring, which is a long-term strategic gain worth preserving.
key_factors: US tariffs on $250B of Chinese goods already in effect, with 25% rate on $200B tranche
UNCTAD study: $35B Chinese export loss but US consumers bearing heaviest cost burden
White House adviser Kudlow: 'both sides will suffer'
IMF cut global growth forecasts citing trade tensions
US core demands (IP protection, market access, end forced tech transfer) remain unresolved
Trade diversion of $21B to third countries (Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, EU) partially offsets Chinese losses
Phase 1 negotiations ongoing; premature concession would waste leverage
US trade deficit with China at $419B; structural issues persist

sources_cited.excerpt: US tariffs caused a 25% export loss, inflicting a US$35 billion blow to Chinese exports in the US market for tariffed goods in the first half of 2019. Consumers in the US are bearing the heaviest brunt of the US tariffs on China.
White House economic adviser Larry Kudlow said Sunday that 'both sides will pay,' noting that the tariffs will cause China to suffer GDP losses as its export market diminishes.

Consumers will pay more for many products, from fish and furniture to vitamins and virtual reality headsets. Chinese auto parts are found in many cars and some estimate new cars will cost $1,000 to $3,000 more.

The US also wants China to buy more US goods to rein in its lofty $419bn trade deficit with China. The International Monetary Fund said the escalation of US-China trade tension was one factor to have contributed to a 'significantly weakened global expansion.'
Sen. Lindsey Graham: 'This is the best chance in my lifetime to get China to change their cheating ways. The tariffs are tools that bring China to the table.'

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should continue engaging in negotiations with the United States while maintaining a firm stance on core interests. We should avoid further escalation that would deepen economic damage, but also resist making unilateral concessions that undermine our development model. A patient, calibrated approach that signals willingness to talk while protecting strategic sectors is the best path forward.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is significant but not existential. UNCTAD data shows US tariffs caused a $35 billion blow to Chinese exports in the US market in H1 2019, with office machinery and communication equipment sectors hit hardest (55% trade decline). However, Chinese firms maintained 75% of their exports to the US despite tariffs, and trade diversion to Vietnam, Taiwan, and Mexico partially offset losses. The yuan fell over 5% against the dollar in 2018 but stabilized in 2019, and the Shanghai Composite recovered 16% YTD. The US has escalated tariffs on $200 billion of goods from 10% to 25% and threatened tariffs on an additional $300 billion, creating real pressure on export hubs and supply chains. However, the US side also bears costs—White House adviser Kudlow acknowledged 'both sides will suffer'—and the IMF has flagged trade tensions as weakening global expansion. China's strategic retaliation on $110 billion of US goods, targeting Republican-district products like soybeans, provides leverage. The negotiation stance is appropriate because: (1) further escalation risks triggering the threatened $300 billion tariff round, which would be far more damaging; (2) the US is also under domestic pressure from consumers and businesses bearing tariff costs; (3) maintaining talks preserves optionality while China accelerates diversification and tech self-sufficiency goals under Made in China 2025.
key_factors: US tariffs on $200bn raised from 10% to 25%, threatening additional $300bn
UNCTAD: $35bn Chinese export loss in H1 2019, but 75% of exports maintained
Trade diversion to Vietnam, Taiwan, Mexico partially offsets losses
US domestic costs acknowledged by White House (Kudlow: 'both sides will suffer')
Shanghai Composite up 16% YTD, yuan stabilized in 2019 after 2018 decline
China's $110bn retaliatory tariffs strategically targeting Republican districts
IMF flagged US-China tensions as factor in weakened global expansion
